about: Concept data for the Study Map (study-map/): build_concepts.py checks it and confirms every place against the tool pages, and the Study Map uses the confirmed places, layers, summaries, other names, and references. Each place names a tool slug from tools.json, a kind (learn, drill, build, fix = troubleshoot, lab), and how to confirm it in the tool's page: where = the tool's own labels joined with ' › ' (every step must appear), find = terms of which at least one must appear. layers: OSI 1 to 7, and host for the machine itself. refs: src is standard or vendor. Never list a place you haven't found in the tool.

concepts.name: OSI model
concepts.summary: A seven-layer map of network communication, from the cable (layer 1) up to the application (layer 7). Use it to say where a problem or a defense lives.

locations.where: Physical › Dead link after the office move
locations.note: Name each ticket's layer before you answer: Physical tickets are layer 1, Switching 2, Addressing 3, Services 7.

refs.title: ITU-T X.200: OSI basic reference model

concepts.name: TCP/IP model
concepts.summary: The four layers the Internet runs on: Link, Internet (IP), Transport (TCP and UDP), and Application. OSI layers 5 to 7 fold into Application.

locations.where: Services › Websites fail, the internet works
locations.note: Sort the tickets into TCP/IP layers: Link (Physical and Switching), Internet (Addressing), and Application (Services).

concepts.name: Encapsulation
concepts.summary: Each layer wraps the data in its own header: a segment (layer 4) rides inside a packet (layer 3), which rides inside a frame (layer 2). The receiver unwraps them in reverse.

locations.note: Each router subinterface adds an 802.1Q VLAN tag to its frames: encapsulation you configure by hand.

concepts.name: Confidentiality, integrity, and availability
concepts.summary: The three things defense protects. A good fix raises one without breaking another, which is why you never disable a service the machine is supposed to provide.

locations.note: The Progress Check includes availability checks, so breaking a service the scenario needs shows up right away.

concepts.name: Least privilege
concepts.summary: Give each account only the rights its job needs, and no more. Most account fixes are least-privilege fixes.

locations.note: Compare group members with the scenario brief's list of who should be an administrator.

concepts.name: Defense in depth
concepts.summary: Stack independent defenses, such as accounts, firewall, services, and updates, so that one miss doesn't expose the whole system.

locations.note: After a scenario, sort your fixes into accounts, policy, services, firewall, and updates. Which layer did you skip?

concepts.name: Baselines and checklists
concepts.summary: A baseline is the known-good configuration; a checklist turns it into steps, so you harden the same way every time and can show what you changed.

locations.note: Build your own hardening checklist and study plan.

concepts.name: Binary and decimal
concepts.summary: An IPv4 address is 32 bits written as four 8-bit octets. Converting an octet with the place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, and 1 is the root skill of subnetting.

concepts.name: IPv4 addresses, masks, and prefixes
concepts.summary: The mask, or /prefix, splits an address into network bits and host bits. /24 is 255.255.255.0: 24 network bits and 8 host bits.

locations.note: Slide the prefix and watch network bits and host bits trade places.

concepts.name: Network, broadcast, and host range
concepts.summary: For any address and prefix, the network address has all host bits set to 0, the broadcast has them all set to 1, and the usable hosts sit in between.

locations.where: Addressing › The router rejects the new LAN address

concepts.name: Right-sizing subnets and VLSM
concepts.summary: Pick the smallest prefix that fits each host count, then carve the block largest-first so no two subnets overlap.

refs.title: RFC 1878: Variable length subnet table for IPv4

concepts.name: Wildcard masks
concepts.summary: The inverse of the subnet mask: subtract each octet from 255. ACLs use it to say which address bits must match.

refs.title: Cisco: Configure commonly used IP ACLs

concepts.name: Private, public, and link-local addresses
concepts.summary: 10/8, 172.16/12, and 192.168/16 are private and never route on the Internet. A 169.254.x.x (APIPA) address means the host gave up waiting for DHCP.

refs.title: RFC 1918: Address allocation for private internets
RFC 3927: Dynamic configuration of IPv4 link-local addresses

concepts.name: IPv6 addresses
concepts.summary: 128-bit addresses written as eight groups of hex. To shorten one, drop the leading zeros in each group, then replace the longest run of all-zero groups with :: once.

locations.where: Quick fire › IPv6 compress and expand

concepts.name: Switches and MAC addresses
concepts.summary: A switch forwards frames by MAC address inside one broadcast domain, learning which address lives on which port.

concepts.name: VLANs and access ports
concepts.summary: VLANs split one switch into separate broadcast domains. Put each user port in its VLAN as an access port, and leave VLAN 1 unused.

locations.note: The S1 tasks: VLANs 10, 20, 99, and 999 with their names, then the access ports.

locations.where: Switching › Wrong subnet on one desk

concepts.name: Trunks and 802.1Q tagging
concepts.summary: A trunk carries many VLANs over one link by tagging frames. Set it statically, give it an unused native VLAN, and allow only the VLANs that need to cross.

locations.note: The S1 G0/1 tasks: static trunk, native VLAN, and allowed list.

locations.where: Switching › Management VLAN dies at the trunk
Switching › A warning keeps scrolling on S1

find: Trunk native VLAN moved to an unused VLAN

locations.where: Switching › Principals stuck on their own VLAN

concepts.name: Trunk negotiation (DTP)
concepts.summary: Ports that negotiate trunks let a rogue device become a trunk and reach every VLAN. Hard-set each port to access or trunk, and turn negotiation off.

concepts.name: Port security
concepts.summary: Limit which and how many MAC addresses may use a port. Depending on the mode, a violation drops the traffic, logs it, or shuts the port.

locations.note: Then move a PC's cable to another port and watch the violation.

concepts.name: PortFast and BPDU Guard
concepts.summary: PortFast lets a port to an end device forward right away. BPDU Guard shuts that port if a switch appears on it, protecting the spanning tree.

find: BPDU Guard on every PortFast port

locations.where: Physical › Classroom port died when a spare switch went in

concepts.name: Switch management address (SVI)
concepts.summary: You reach a switch through a VLAN interface (SVI) with its own IP address and default gateway. Use a dedicated management VLAN, not VLAN 1.

locations.where: Switching › Cannot manage the new switch
Switching › Manageable from only one subnet

concepts.name: Shut down unused ports
concepts.summary: Every live, unused port is a free plug-in for an intruder. Shut it down and move it out of VLAN 1.

concepts.name: DHCP snooping
concepts.summary: Only trusted ports may answer DHCP requests, so a rogue server can't hand clients a malicious gateway or DNS server.

concepts.name: Default gateway
concepts.summary: A host sends anything outside its own subnet to its default gateway. A wrong gateway means local traffic works and remote traffic doesn't.

locations.where: Addressing › Local works, remote does not
Addressing › The gateway looks right, but is not

concepts.name: Static and default routes
concepts.summary: A router only reaches networks it knows about. A default route (0.0.0.0/0) sends everything else upstream, a host route (/32) names exactly one address, and OSPF can share a static route with its neighbours through redistribute static subnets.

locations.where: Device config › Everything inside works, the internet does not

locations.note: The host route to 8.8.8.8 and OSPF redistribute static subnets.

locations.where: Config accuracy › Site B loses 8.8.8.8 in the failover test

locations.note: Level 4, Two sites: RtrB shares its host route with RtrA through OSPF.

refs.title: RFC 1812: Requirements for IP version 4 routers

concepts.name: Routing between VLANs
concepts.summary: One router port carries a subinterface per VLAN, each tagged with dot1Q and acting as that VLAN's default gateway.

locations.note: The R1 subinterface tasks: G0/0.10, G0/0.20, and G0/0.99 as the native VLAN.

Device config › The gateway tags the wrong VLAN

concepts.name: DHCP
concepts.summary: DHCP leases addresses from a pool. Exclude the addresses you assign by hand, and relay requests across a router with ip helper-address.

locations.where: Services › DHCP server on another subnet

concepts.name: DNS
concepts.summary: DNS turns names into addresses. When addresses work but names don't, suspect DNS.

locations.where: Services › Websites fail, the internet works

refs.title: RFC 1034: Domain names, concepts and facilities

concepts.name: TCP, UDP, and port numbers
concepts.summary: TCP sets up a reliable connection; UDP just sends. The port number names the service: 22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 80 and 443 web, 3389 Remote Desktop.

locations.note: Telnet on port 23 against SSH on port 22.
Firewall rules name a port and a protocol, such as 22/tcp.

refs.title: IANA service name and port number registry

concepts.name: Access control lists (ACLs)
concepts.summary: An ordered list of permit and deny rules that ends in an implicit deny. Where you apply it, and in which direction, decides what it actually filters.

locations.where: Access lists › The ACL is applied, Students still get through

concepts.name: Privileged mode: enable secret
concepts.summary: enable secret stores a hash of the password; enable password stores it in plain text or as weak type 7. When both exist, the secret wins.

refs.title: Cisco Guide to Harden Cisco IOS Devices

concepts.name: Password encryption and type 7
concepts.summary: service password-encryption only scrambles plain-text passwords into type 7, which anyone can reverse. Real protection is secrets (hashes) and keeping the config private.

refs.title: Cisco Guide to Harden Cisco IOS Devices

concepts.name: Console and VTY lines
concepts.summary: Every way into a device needs a sign-in: console and VTY lines need authentication and an idle timeout.

find: VTY lines 5 to 15 need no login at all

locations.where: Remote access › Password required, but none set

refs.title: Cisco Guide to Harden Cisco IOS Devices

concepts.name: SSH-only remote management
concepts.summary: Telnet sends passwords in clear text. SSH needs a hostname, a domain name, RSA keys, local users, and VTY lines set to SSH only.

locations.where: Remote access › SSH will not start

refs.title: RFC 4251: The Secure Shell (SSH) protocol architecture
Cisco Guide to Harden Cisco IOS Devices

concepts.name: Logging and time sync
concepts.summary: Logs only help if they survive and line up: send them to a syslog server, stamp them with the time, and sync every clock with NTP.

concepts.name: SNMP community strings
concepts.summary: SNMP v1 and v2c community strings are clear-text passwords. Defaults like public and private let anyone read, or even change, the device.

refs.title: RFC 3414: User-based security model for SNMPv3

concepts.name: Running and startup configuration
concepts.summary: Changes live in RAM (the running-config) until you save them to NVRAM (the startup-config). Unsaved fixes disappear on the next reload.

concepts.name: User account audit
concepts.summary: Compare the accounts on the machine with the list of people who should have one, then remove or disable everyone else.

concepts.name: Administrator and sudo rights
concepts.summary: Only the listed admins belong in Administrators, sudo, or wheel. Every extra admin is a full-control account an attacker can use.

concepts.name: Guest, built-in, and root accounts
concepts.summary: Disable the Guest account, lock down the built-in Administrator, and block direct root logins. Attackers try these names first.

concepts.name: Password policy
concepts.summary: Set a minimum length, a history, and a maximum age so weak or reused passwords are refused. Current guidance favors long passphrases over forced complexity.

refs.title: NIST SP 800-63B: Authentication and authenticator management

concepts.name: Account lockout and brute-force protection
concepts.summary: After a few failed sign-ins, lock the account or block logins for a while, so password guessing stalls.

concepts.name: PAM, the Linux sign-in modules
concepts.summary: PAM chains the checks that every Linux sign-in and password change passes through. Password and lockout rules live in /etc/pam.d.

concepts.name: Local Security Policy and Group Policy
concepts.summary: Windows keeps its password, lockout, user-rights, and security-option settings in Local Security Policy. Group Policy applies them to many machines at once.

concepts.name: Audit policy and logs
concepts.summary: Record sign-ins and changes, both successes and failures. Without audit logs you can't tell what happened or when.

concepts.name: User Account Control (UAC)
concepts.summary: Even admins run with standard rights until they approve an elevation prompt. Keep UAC at its default level or higher.

concepts.name: Registry, reg, and secedit
concepts.summary: Most Windows policy settings are registry values. reg reads and sets them one at a time; secedit exports and imports whole security policies.

concepts.name: Legal warning banners
concepts.summary: A banner warns that access is for authorized users only, which supports action against intruders. Never write a welcome.

concepts.name: Disable unneeded services
concepts.summary: Every running service is something to attack. Stop and disable what the machine doesn't need, and keep what the scenario requires.

find: The web management server is on

concepts.name: Legacy Windows features (SMBv1)
concepts.summary: Turn off legacy components such as SMBv1 that attackers abuse. They are features, not services, so they live in a different panel.

refs.title: Microsoft Learn: Detect, enable, and disable SMBv1, SMBv2, and SMBv3

concepts.name: Remove unwanted software
concepts.summary: Inventory what's installed and remove anything that isn't authorized, especially remote-access and hacking tools.

concepts.name: Updates and patching
concepts.summary: Install security updates and turn on automatic updates. Most break-ins use flaws that already have a patch.

refs.title: FreeBSD Handbook: Updating and upgrading FreeBSD

concepts.name: Scheduled tasks and cron jobs
concepts.summary: Attackers schedule their tools to come back after you remove them. Review every task and cron job, and delete what you can't explain.

concepts.name: File permissions
concepts.summary: Sensitive files such as /etc/shadow must be readable only by the accounts that need them. Check owners and modes, not just contents.

concepts.name: Host firewall
concepts.summary: Turn the firewall on, deny inbound connections by default, then allow only the services the machine must offer.

concepts.name: Remote Desktop exposure
concepts.summary: If Remote Desktop isn't required, turn it off. If it is, require Network Level Authentication and limit who may connect.

concepts.name: SSH server settings
concepts.summary: Harden sshd_config on Linux and FreeBSD: no root logins, no empty passwords, and remote access only for the users who need it.

concepts.name: IOS command modes and help
concepts.summary: IOS has modes (>, #, and (config)#), and each command works only in its own mode. Type ? to list what's valid where you are.

locations.where: Device config › The hostname command fails

locations.note: IOS consoles with ? help, abbreviations, and the exact error messages.

concepts.name: cmd and PowerShell
concepts.summary: Chain commands with | and save output with >. One command line can list, filter, and export what a settings panel shows.

locations.note: cmd and PowerShell with pipes and redirection, beside the real panels.

concepts.name: Bash, sudo, and text editors
concepts.summary: Most Linux hardening happens in a terminal: sudo to act as root, pipes and grep to find things, and nano or vi to edit config files.

locations.note: A bash-like terminal with sudo, apt, systemctl, and nano.

concepts.name: Troubleshooting by layer
concepts.summary: Start from the symptom, test layer by layer (link, address, gateway, name), and fix the root cause instead of the symptom.

locations.note: Each ticket: the complaint, real device output, the root cause, then the fix.

concepts.name: Verify with ping, SSH, and show commands
concepts.summary: Prove a fix from the user's side (ping, sign in over SSH, browse) and from the device's own view (show commands) before you call it done.

locations.note: Missions end by proving the result from a PC.
Secure the topology, then prove it with ping.
Each ticket gives you real ipconfig or show output to read.

concepts.name: Scenario briefs and investigation questions
concepts.summary: Read the scenario brief first: it says who is authorized and which services must stay up. Answer the investigation questions before your fixes change the evidence.

concepts.name: Threat actors, motives, and APTs
concepts.summary: Who attacks and why: criminals after money, hacktivists after attention, insiders who already have access, and nation-state groups (APTs) that stay hidden for months. Motive and skill shape what a defender should expect.

concepts.name: Drive-by, watering-hole, and look-alike sites
concepts.summary: Attacks that wait on the web: a drive-by download runs from a booby-trapped page, a watering hole infects a site the targets already trust, and a look-alike domain copies a real name letter by letter.

refs.title: FTC: How to recognize and avoid phishing scams

concepts.name: Zero-days and the patch window
concepts.summary: A zero-day is a flaw attackers use before any fix exists. Once a patch ships, the race is on: attackers study the fix while defenders roll it out, so flaws already being exploited go first.

concepts.name: The kill chain and ATT&CK
concepts.summary: Two maps of an attack: the kill chain's stages from reconnaissance to actions on objectives, and MITRE ATT&CK's catalog of tactics and techniques. Placing evidence on them shows what came before and what to look for next.

concepts.name: Threat intelligence and indicators
concepts.summary: Shared knowledge about attackers: indicators of compromise (file hashes, domains, and addresses) to block or hunt for, and attacker behavior, which lasts longer than any single indicator. TLP labels say how far a report may be shared.

concepts.name: Recognizing attack tools by their traces
concepts.summary: Common attack tools leave recognizable marks: a burst of connections across many ports, a wave of failed sign-ins spread across many accounts, or a credential dumper reading LSASS memory. Recognize the trace, then ask what the attacker wanted.

concepts.name: On-path, spoofing, and flooding attacks
concepts.summary: Attacks on the network itself: an on-path attacker sits between two hosts (often by ARP spoofing), spoofed packets fake their source, and floods exhaust a link or a server (DoS and DDoS).

concepts.name: Evil twins, rogue access points, and deauthentication
concepts.summary: Wireless attacks: an evil twin copies a trusted network name, a rogue access point plugs an unapproved radio into the wired network, and forged deauthentication frames knock clients off so they reconnect to the attacker.

concepts.name: Checking emails, links, and files before you trust them
concepts.summary: Check before you trust: read the real sender and the SPF, DKIM, and DMARC results in the headers, read where a link really goes before you click, and look up a file's hash before you open it.

refs.title: FTC: How to recognize and avoid phishing scams
RFC 7489: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC)

concepts.name: AI tools, data you paste, and prompt injection
concepts.summary: Anything pasted into an AI tool may be stored or reused, so keep private data out. AI answers can be confidently wrong, and text hidden in a page or file can carry instructions that hijack the tool (prompt injection).

refs.title: OWASP GenAI Security Project: Prompt Injection

concepts.name: Symmetric and asymmetric keys
concepts.summary: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key and is fast (AES); asymmetric encryption uses a key pair, where the public key locks and only the matching private key unlocks (RSA). Real systems use both.

concepts.name: Digital signatures and code signing
concepts.summary: A digital signature is a hash sealed with the signer's private key; anyone with the public key can check who signed and that nothing changed since. Code signing applies the same check to programs and updates.

concepts.name: Certificates and the chain of trust
concepts.summary: A certificate binds a name to a public key and is signed by a certificate authority. A browser follows the chain from the site's certificate up to a trusted root and checks the name, the dates, and every signature.

refs.title: RFC 5280: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and CRL Profile

concepts.name: TLS and HTTPS
concepts.summary: TLS wraps a connection in encryption after the server proves its identity with a certificate; HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS. The padlock means the connection is private and the name matched, not that the site is honest.

refs.title: RFC 8446: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

concepts.name: Salted password hashes
concepts.summary: Systems store a slow, salted hash of each password instead of the password itself. The salt makes identical passwords hash differently, so precomputed tables fail and every guess costs time.

concepts.name: Single sign-on and directories
concepts.summary: With single sign-on, one identity provider checks who you are and hands each app a signed token, so accounts, MFA, and offboarding live in one directory instead of in every app.

concepts.name: LANs, WANs, wireless links, and topologies
concepts.summary: A LAN joins devices in one place, a WAN links places together, and Wi-Fi is a wireless LAN. Topology is the shape of the links: star, mesh, or a mix.

concepts.name: NAT and the home router
concepts.summary: Network address translation lets many devices with private addresses share one public address: the router rewrites each outgoing connection and keeps a table to send replies back. Unrequested inbound traffic finds no entry unless a port is forwarded.

refs.title: RFC 3022: Traditional IP Network Address Translator (Traditional NAT)

concepts.name: Wi-Fi security modes and router settings
concepts.summary: Choose WPA3 (or WPA2 with AES) and a long passphrase, turn off WPS, put guests on their own network, change the router's admin password, and keep its firmware current.

concepts.name: The TCP handshake, flags, and ICMP
concepts.summary: TCP opens with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK and closes with FIN or an abrupt RST, so the flags tell you who started a connection and how it ended. ICMP carries the network's own messages, such as echo (ping) and unreachable.

concepts.name: Port states and scan results
concepts.summary: A port scan reports each port as open (a service answered), closed (the host answered that nothing listens), or filtered (no answer, usually a firewall). Compare the open list with what should be running.

concepts.name: Clear-text protocols and their protected forms
concepts.summary: Telnet, FTP, plain HTTP, and older SNMP send passwords and data as clear text that anyone on the path can read. Use the protected forms instead: SSH, SFTP or FTPS, HTTPS, LDAPS, and SNMPv3.

concepts.name: Firewall types, zones, and the DMZ
concepts.summary: Network firewalls split a network into zones of trust. Public-facing servers sit in a DMZ (a screened subnet), so a break-in there doesn't reach the inside, and rules deny by default and allow only the flows each zone needs.

concepts.name: VPNs and IPsec
concepts.summary: A VPN carries traffic through an encrypted tunnel across a network you don't trust: site-to-site joins two offices, and remote access joins one laptop. IPsec is a common tunnel protocol.

concepts.name: 802.1X, RADIUS, and network access control
concepts.summary: Network access control checks a device before it joins: 802.1X makes the switch port or the Wi-Fi ask for credentials, and a RADIUS server decides whether to let it in and which VLAN it lands on.

concepts.name: Zero trust design
concepts.summary: Zero trust drops the idea of a trusted inside: every request is checked for identity, device health, and need, every time, and access is limited to the one resource asked for.

concepts.name: Antivirus, EDR, and SIEM
concepts.summary: Antivirus blocks known-bad files; EDR records what every process does so analysts can trace and stop an attack; a SIEM gathers logs from many systems into one place to search them and raise alerts.

concepts.name: IDS and IPS
concepts.summary: An intrusion detection system watches traffic and alerts; an intrusion prevention system sits inline and can drop what matches. Both use signatures for known attacks and baselines to flag the unusual.

concepts.name: True and false positives
concepts.summary: Every alert is a guess: a true positive caught real trouble, a false positive cried wolf, and a false negative is the attack nobody saw. Tuning a detection trades one kind of mistake for the other.

concepts.name: Windows events and logon types
concepts.summary: Windows records security activity as numbered events: 4624 a successful logon, 4625 a failed one, 4688 a new process. The logon type in each logon event says how the user arrived: at the keyboard (2), over the network (3), or by Remote Desktop (10).

refs.title: Microsoft Learn: Events to monitor in Active Directory

concepts.name: Syslog, auth.log, and the journal
concepts.summary: Linux and FreeBSD log through syslog into files under /var/log, such as auth.log for sign-ins and sudo; systemd systems also keep a journal you read with journalctl.

concepts.name: Reading firewall log lines
concepts.summary: A firewall log line records a decision: the time, the action (allow or drop), the protocol, the source and destination addresses, and the ports. Read them for scans, blocked probes, and traffic that should never have been allowed.

concepts.name: Packet captures and flow records
concepts.summary: A packet capture saves every byte that crossed a link, for close reading in Wireshark or tcpdump; a flow record keeps only who talked to whom, when, and how much, so it scales to a whole network.

concepts.name: Alert triage and severity
concepts.summary: Triage decides which alert to work first: confirm it is real, judge how much is at stake and how fast it is spreading, set a severity, and escalate or close it with a note.

concepts.name: Incident response phases
concepts.summary: Incident response runs in phases: prepare, detect and analyze, contain, eradicate, recover, and learn. Following them keeps a team from wiping evidence or declaring victory too soon.

concepts.name: Containment, eradication, and recovery
concepts.summary: Containment stops the spread (isolate the host, disable the account, block the address); eradication removes the foothold and every persistence point; recovery restores from clean backups and watches for a return.

concepts.name: Evidence handling and order of volatility
concepts.summary: Collect the most fleeting evidence first (memory and network connections before the disk), hash every copy, work only on copies, and log each hand-off in a chain of custody so the findings hold up.

refs.title: RFC 3227: Guidelines for Evidence Collection and Archiving

concepts.name: Timelines from many logs
concepts.summary: Merge events from every source onto one timeline in one time zone (UTC) to see the order of an attack. Check each source's clock first: a few minutes of skew can reverse cause and effect.

concepts.name: Sandboxes and file reputation
concepts.summary: A sandbox runs a suspicious file in a throwaway machine and records what it does; a reputation lookup checks the file's hash against what others have seen. Neither proves a file safe: new or evasive samples can pass both.

concepts.name: Threat hunting
concepts.summary: Hunting starts from a hypothesis (if an attacker did this, what trace would it leave?) and searches for that trace before any alert fires. Each hunt either finds something or becomes a new detection.

concepts.name: Detection rules, playbooks, and automation
concepts.summary: A detection rule turns a pattern into an alert; a playbook says, step by step, what to do when it fires; automation (SOAR) runs the safe, repetitive steps so people can focus on judgment.

concepts.name: Stakeholders, lessons learned, and the report
concepts.summary: After an incident, tell each stakeholder what they need (facts for leaders, steps for staff, and any notice the law requires), then hold a blameless review that turns what went wrong into owned, dated fixes.

concepts.name: Honeypots and sinkholes
concepts.summary: Deception plants things no legitimate user should touch, such as a honeypot server, a honeytoken credential, or a canary file, so any touch is a high-confidence alert. A DNS sinkhole points known-bad names at a safe address to catch infected hosts.

concepts.name: Reading a process list from memory
concepts.summary: A memory image captures what was running: processes, network connections, and loaded code, including malware that never touched the disk. Compare the process list from memory with what the live system reported to spot what was hidden.

concepts.name: HTTP requests, responses, and cookies
concepts.summary: A browser sends an HTTP request (a method such as GET or POST, a path, and headers); the server answers with a status code such as 200 or 404, headers, and a body. Cookies carry a session from one request to the next.

concepts.name: Reading a link: who owns it
concepts.summary: The owner of a link is its registered domain: the name just before the first single slash, read from the right (the part like example.com). Everything to its left is a subdomain the owner chose, so a trusted name there proves nothing.

refs.title: RFC 3986: Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax

concepts.name: Web attacks in access logs
concepts.summary: A web server's access log shows each request: address, time, method, path, status, and user agent. Attacks stand out as odd paths and parameters: quote marks and SQL words, script tags, ../ sequences, or one address requesting thousands of pages.

refs.title: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

concepts.name: Input handling and memory safety
concepts.summary: Treat every input as data, never as code: parameterized queries stop SQL injection, output encoding stops cross-site scripting, and memory-safe languages remove whole classes of overflow bugs.

refs.title: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
CISA: The Case for Memory Safe Roadmaps

concepts.name: Broken access control
concepts.summary: Broken access control lets a user act outside their permissions, for example by changing an ID in a URL to read someone else's record. The server must check authorization on every request, not just hide the button.

concepts.name: Cloud service and deployment models
concepts.summary: Service models say how much the provider runs for you: the infrastructure (IaaS), a platform (PaaS), or the whole application (SaaS). Deployment models say who shares it: public, private, hybrid, or community cloud.

refs.title: NIST SP 800-145: The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing

concepts.name: Who secures what in the cloud
concepts.summary: The provider secures the cloud itself (buildings, hardware, and its own services); the customer secures what they put in it: accounts, data, settings, and, in IaaS, the operating system. The split moves with the service model.

concepts.name: Cloud policies, storage, and network rules
concepts.summary: Cloud access is written as policy: who may do which action on which resource. Most cloud breaches trace back to a policy that grants too much, a storage bucket left public, or a network rule open to the whole internet.

refs.title: AWS: Security best practices in IAM

concepts.name: Cloud audit logs and leaked keys
concepts.summary: Cloud audit logs record every API call: who made it, from where, and what changed. A leaked access key shows up as calls from a new place or at an odd hour: revoke the key first, then read the log to see what it did.

concepts.name: Infrastructure as code, containers, and functions
concepts.summary: Infrastructure as code describes servers, networks, and policies in files that can be reviewed and scanned before anything is built. Containers and serverless functions shrink what runs, but their images, permissions, and secrets still need checking.

concepts.name: Isolation, from processes to air gaps
concepts.summary: Isolation limits what a compromise can reach: separate processes and users, containers, virtual machines, network segments, and, at the far end, an air gap with no network link at all.

concepts.name: Reading and writing defender scripts
concepts.summary: A short script repeats a check the same way every time: loop over users, files, or log lines, test each one, and print what needs attention. Read any script before you run it, especially one downloaded and piped straight into a shell.

concepts.name: JSON, YAML, and CSV
concepts.summary: Logs, settings, and exports often arrive as structured text: JSON (nested keys and values), YAML (the same idea, set out by indentation), and CSV (rows and columns). Parse them with a tool instead of by eye.

concepts.name: macOS security basics
concepts.summary: macOS is Unix underneath, so Terminal habits from Linux carry over. Its own layers: Gatekeeper checks downloaded apps, FileVault encrypts the disk, XProtect blocks known malware, and System Integrity Protection guards system files.

concepts.name: AppArmor, SELinux, and systemd sandboxing
concepts.summary: Confinement limits what a service can touch even if it is taken over: AppArmor profiles and SELinux policies list the files and actions it may use, and systemd options such as ProtectSystem and NoNewPrivileges fence a unit in.

concepts.name: auditd and file integrity
concepts.summary: auditd records chosen system calls and file accesses (watch /etc/passwd, log every sudo), and ausearch reads them back. A file integrity checker such as AIDE hashes key files and reports any change.

concepts.name: Disk encryption and secure boot
concepts.summary: Full-disk encryption (BitLocker, LUKS, or GELI) keeps a lost or stolen drive unreadable; Secure Boot and the TPM check that the startup code has not been tampered with. Keep the recovery key somewhere other than the device.

concepts.name: Reading process trees
concepts.summary: Every process has a parent. A tree shows the chain, so odd pairings stand out: a word processor that starts PowerShell, or a web server that starts a shell, usually means someone took control of the parent.

concepts.name: Unique local admin passwords (LAPS)
concepts.summary: If every PC shares one local administrator password, one stolen hash opens them all. Windows LAPS gives each machine its own random local admin password, rotates it, and stores it in the directory for authorized admins only.

concepts.name: PowerShell logging and AMSI
concepts.summary: Script block logging (event 4104) records the PowerShell code that actually ran, even after obfuscation is peeled away, and AMSI lets antivirus inspect scripts as they run. Turn both on with Group Policy.

concepts.name: Application control and ASR rules
concepts.summary: Application control flips the default so only approved programs run (App Control for Business or AppLocker). Attack surface reduction rules block specific risky behaviors, such as Office apps starting child processes.

refs.title: Microsoft Learn: Application Control for Windows

concepts.name: Admin tiers and jump servers
concepts.summary: Keep the most powerful accounts on the most protected machines: domain admins sign in only to domain controllers and dedicated admin workstations, and admins reach servers through a hardened jump server instead of from everyday PCs.

concepts.name: Domain, Entra, and hybrid device join
concepts.summary: A domain-joined PC trusts the on-site Active Directory; an Entra-joined PC trusts Microsoft's cloud directory and is managed with Intune; hybrid join registers it in both. Where a device is joined decides where its policies and sign-ins come from.

concepts.name: NTLM and Kerberos sign-in
concepts.summary: In a domain, Kerberos signs users in with tickets from the domain controller instead of sending password hashes around; NTLM is the older challenge-and-response fallback. Watch for NTLM where Kerberos should be used.

refs.title: Microsoft Learn: Events to monitor in Active Directory

concepts.name: Credential theft and its defenses
concepts.summary: Attackers dump password hashes and tickets from memory (LSASS) and reuse them to move between machines. Credential Guard, LSA protection, the Protected Users group, and fewer admin sign-ins shrink what there is to steal.

refs.title: Microsoft Learn: Configure added LSA protection
Microsoft Learn: Protected Users security group

concepts.name: Built-in tools misused
concepts.summary: Attackers prefer tools already on the system (certutil, mshta, rundll32, PowerShell) because they are signed, trusted, and rarely trip antivirus. Watch how and by whom they are started, not just whether they exist.

concepts.name: Rating and treating risk
concepts.summary: Risk combines likelihood and impact. Rate each finding on both, record it in a risk register, and choose a treatment: reduce it, transfer it (insurance or a contract), avoid it by stopping the activity, or accept it with a signature.

refs.title: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2: Risk Management Framework

concepts.name: Vulnerability management
concepts.summary: Vulnerability management is a loop: find flaws (scans and advisories), rank them by severity, exposure, and whether attackers already use them (the KEV catalog), fix or mitigate them, then scan again to prove it.

concepts.name: Security frameworks
concepts.summary: Frameworks are shared outlines for a whole security program: the NIST Cybersecurity Framework groups the work into Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover; the CIS Controls rank practical safeguards; and ISO/IEC 27001 can be certified by an auditor.

concepts.name: Laws, compliance, and auditors
concepts.summary: Laws and contracts set minimums: FERPA protects student records, COPPA children's data online, HIPAA health records, and PCI DSS card data. Compliance means showing an auditor the evidence that the required controls actually run.

refs.title: US Department of Education: Student Privacy
FTC: Children’s Online Privacy Protection Rule

concepts.name: Data classification and loss prevention
concepts.summary: Label data by how much harm its exposure would cause (public, internal, confidential, restricted), then protect each label to match. Data loss prevention watches email, uploads, and USB drives for labeled or sensitive data on its way out.

concepts.name: Access control models: DAC, MAC, RBAC, and ABAC
concepts.summary: Who decides access: in DAC the owner shares as they like; in MAC the system enforces labels nobody can override; RBAC grants access by job role; and ABAC weighs attributes such as department, device, and time.

concepts.name: Threat modeling with STRIDE
concepts.summary: Threat modeling asks what could go wrong before it does: draw how data flows and where it crosses trust boundaries, then walk each part through STRIDE (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, and elevation of privilege).

concepts.name: Roles, certifications, and practice
concepts.summary: Security work spans many roles: analyst, engineer, tester, auditor, and responder, each described in the NICE Framework. Entry certifications such as ISC2 CC and CompTIA Security+ check the basics, and legal practice ranges and capture-the-flag games build the skill.

concepts.name: Responsible disclosure
concepts.summary: Found a flaw in someone else's system? Stop, explore no further, and report it privately through their published channel (a security.txt file or a disclosure policy), then give them time to fix it before anyone goes public.
